newsitem.title: UK: International LPG falls, demand low in Europe/Asia.
newsitem.headline: International LPG falls, demand low in Europe/Asia.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices continued their decline this week as slack demand from Europe and East Asia failed to support levels already coming down at the end of the northern hemisphere winter.

In Northwest Europe, a 7,000 to 10,000 tonne propane cargo was reported sold for $200 a tonne cif France for delivery any time in March. This followed a deal the previous week which had been concluded at $266 a tonne cif Lavera or $260 a tonne cif Northwest Europe at buyers' option, and shows the speed with which the price is still coming down.

"It's crashed a little bit again this week," said a Scandinavian trader. After the deal at $260, he said, "naphtha came down, the outlook for March became softer and then this deal came along. This new level is representative of the market."

He added that there is expected to be some cracking demand for propane during March, but petrochemical buyers will not come into the market unless the propane price is significantly below the naphtha price. This was assessed in the range $197/199 a tonne cif NWE at midday on Friday.

The market was awaiting the announcement of BP's agreed price, or BPAP, on Friday afternoon. This is the benchmark price for much Northwest European trade, and the company said it hoped to get it out late in the day.

While North Sea propane looks bearish, the butane market was better balanced, dealers said, and there was less potential for a further slide. A 7,000 to 10,000 tonne butane cargo was reported traded at $218 a tonne cif NWE for first half March delivery, and this level was described as "sustainable" by a trader who said the market was "balanced to short." There is demand for North Sea material in Turkey and Spain in March, further supporting levels.

Seagoing coasters in Northwest Europe were quiet and thin, with propane pegged around $220 a tonne fob NWE and butane around $200 a tonne, but the market was described as "inactive." Propane coasters have not yet fallen to catch up with the drops on the cargo market, leading one coaster trader to say that "when it starts to go down it could go down with a bang."

There was some propane interest seen in the Mediterranean. A small piece of less than 10,000 tonnes was sold at above $240 a tonne cif Lavera early in the week, and the seller said there were more opportunities for small cargoes.

With the Saudi Contract Price, or CP, announced during the week at $270 a tonne for propane and $277 for butane, there was interest in moving propane from the north, where prices are much lower, to the Mediterranean where the CP is more of an influence.

The Mediterranean butane market was more opaque, with the price differential between chemical grade and commercial grade seen widening. Chemical grade was valued at around $270 a tonne cif Lavera, while olefinic commercial grade was talked in the low $200's a tonne. With the market relatively thin, at least one major seller was more interested in moving product to the US than selling into the local market.

Algerian state Sonatrach said on Friday that it would not be publishing its official March price until Saturday. A trader declined to give any clues on the level, except to say that it would be "lower than the CP but higher than BPAP."

In the Asian market, discounts to the CP for fob Gulf liftings deepened as the CP was higher than many had anticipated. "The discount is more than $20 a tonne," said a trader. And with such a deep discount on a fob Saudi Arabia basis, premiums to the CP on a C+F Japan basis fell to single figures.

In Japan, discussion was heard around CP +$5/$9 C+F for both propane and butane, but demand remained slim. Some individual companies may need product now, said a trader, but Japan as a whole has sufficient supplies and there is no urgency to purchase.
Price levels of around CP + $30/40 a tonne C+F South China were discussed but demand was thin there as it was in South Korea, a trader said.

The first of the three monthly Saudi tenders, the March T1 tender, was due to close on Friday, with bids valid until next Tuesday. As news of this emerges on to the market next week, it is expected to give some more direction, but until then the market East of Suez remains illiquid.
